title: A vendor-agnostic Secrets Manager, driven by a repo-root manifest, is the project's single source of truth for secret material
context: Every non-trivial project depends on secret material: API keys for third-party vendors, database passwords, signing keys, session salts. The failure modes accumulate quietly: dependency shape lives in whichever file happened to read it, rotation policies are unenforced, laptop-local `.env` files diverge from the deployed environment, agent workflows echo values into transcripts that persist forever. A single source-of-truth model addresses the root cause: one manifest, one client, one audit stream, one boundary the vendor lives behind. This topic is scoped as a project-level global because a composing blueprint that holds a different opinion about the secrets source (a vendor-specific opinionated blueprint, a config-server pattern, a plaintext-committed pattern for a public reference project) needs to conflict here and be resolved by the operator.
decision: The project's secrets source is a Secrets Manager client (TAC-901) reading a repo-root manifest (`secrets.yaml`, TAC-902) that declares every secret by name, per-environment path, owner, rotation-days budget, and required-or-optional. Values live only in the vendor the client resolves against; the manifest carries names and metadata only. Every runtime path that reads a secret value imports the Secrets Manager module and no other; every CI path that gates on secret age or shape reads the manifest and no other. The vendor is pluggable; the interface is not. The default vendor is named in ADR-902; alternatives supersede this ADR at the project level.
consequences: One place to change vendors, one place to audit, one place to enforce least-privilege. The manifest becomes a piece of documentation the project maintains as part of its normal change flow, which is the intended cost. Rotation and access-audit surfaces exist because the client is the sole entry point. Composition with a blueprint that would import a vendor SDK directly conflicts here by design; the operator supersedes with a project-level ADR that either accepts the composed blueprint's shape or restates this one's.

alternativesConsidered.name: Environment-variable-first with no manifest
alternativesConsidered.summary: Every module reads `process.env.X` (or the language equivalent); the shape of the dependency graph is whatever the code paths do.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: This is the default state most projects drift into and the state this blueprint exists to end. Rotation is unenforced, dependency-shape drift goes unnoticed until a deploy breaks, and there is no audit surface for who read what.

alternativesConsidered.name: Per-deployable manifest instead of a single repo-root manifest
alternativesConsidered.summary: Each deployable owns its own secrets file; there is no project-wide view.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: The estate-wide view is the point. Rotation policies and least-privilege audits need one file to look at; per-deployable files split the truth and re-open the drift class.

alternativesConsidered.name: Vendor-committed opinionated blueprint (HashiCorp Vault only, or AWS Secrets Manager only)
alternativesConsidered.summary: Ship the blueprint tied to one specific vendor SDK; the manifest is that vendor's native shape.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Locks the project to a vendor at the blueprint layer, which the doctrine of round-2 refuses (vendor default belongs at ADR-902, contract belongs here). A composing blueprint or a project that wants a different vendor can only escape by removing this blueprint. Splitting the contract from the default keeps both moves available.
